name: Cash Flow Forecasting
title: Cash Flow Forecasting
answer: Cash flow forecasting covers the projection of a company's future cash receipts and payments over chosen horizons, from daily to multi-year. It includes operating, investing and financing cash flows, and it supports liquidity planning, working capital management and funding decisions. The work sits in treasury and liquidity, and it connects to accounting, financial planning and risk. Forecasts may be direct, built from expected invoices and payment runs, or indirect, derived from projected profit and loss and balance sheet movements. The scope also includes scenario and sensitivity analysis, because cash timing is uncertain.

sections.body: Cash flow forecasting covers the projection of a company's future cash receipts and payments over chosen horizons, from daily to multi-year. It includes operating, investing and financing cash flows, and it supports liquidity planning, working capital management and funding decisions. The work sits in treasury and liquidity, and it connects to accounting, financial planning and risk. The scope also includes scenario and sensitivity analysis, because cash timing is uncertain.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The forecasts run on a mix of core systems and specialist tools. ERP and treasury management systems hold the ledger, bank account and payment data, and bank feeds or open banking APIs bring in actual balances and transactions. Spreadsheets remain common for modelling and reconciliation, while cloud data warehouses and planning platforms handle larger volumes and collaboration. AI and machine learning components may sit alongside these systems, drawing on the same data pipelines.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with data collection and reconciliation, pulling actual cash positions, historical flows and expected receipts and payments. Analysts then build driver-based models, linking cash to sales, purchasing, payroll and tax calendars, and they may use statistical methods or machine learning to capture seasonality and payment behaviour. Rolling forecasts are updated regularly, often weekly or monthly, and variance analysis compares forecast to actual to improve the next cycle. Scenario and stress testing are common, because a single point forecast hides the range of possible outcomes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers data lineage, model documentation and audit trails, so that every forecast can be traced back to its sources and assumptions. Internal controls, segregation of duties and approval workflows protect against error and fraud, and they support external audit and regulatory reporting. Data privacy and consent matter when customer or supplier payment data is used, and third-party data feeds need clear contractual rights. Model risk management is important, because a cash forecast can influence borrowing, investment and hedging decisions, so validation and explainability are part of the control framework.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more frequent and more automated forecasting, with real-time or near real-time cash visibility. Machine learning is being applied to payment behaviour prediction and anomaly detection, and scenario planning is becoming more dynamic. Integration with payments, open banking and treasury APIs is likely to reduce manual data handling. Explainability and auditability will remain central as regulators and auditors ask how a forecast was produced.
